scenario_stem:
Fernbrook Cleaning Co is a private limited company in Country X that has sold liquid laundry detergent for 9 years. It employs 34 staff and last year generated revenue of $2.3 million from 18,000 households. The company is now developing a concentrated detergent refill tablet designed to dissolve in existing bottles at home. Demand for low-waste refill solutions is growing across Country X as households try to cut plastic use.

Development has so far cost $260,000, covering laboratory testing, safety certification and pack design, with a further $150,000 needed for a factory trial run. The tablet will retail at $6.50 for a 3-month supply, but 4 of 30 trial households said the tablets dissolved too slowly. The directors must decide whether to proceed to a national launch in March or abandon the project.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'new product development'.
questions.model_answer: New product development is the process by which a business creates, tests and launches new products or significantly improves existing ones, moving from idea generation through design, testing and test marketing to commercial launch. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies new product development as creating or improving products
Refers to stages such as idea generation, testing or launch

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernbrook Cleaning Co might benefit from launching the refill tablet.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Developing a new product can meet changing customer needs and attract new customers [k]; the refill tablet is aimed at 18,000 households already using Fernbrook's liquid detergent, so launching it could capture that base with a more convenient, eco-friendly option [app]. Reason 2: A successful new product can increase revenue and give a competitive advantage [k]; since the tablet will retail at $6.50 for a 3-month supply, a national launch could add a profitable line on top of Fernbrook's $2.3 million revenue base [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises a new product can meet changing customer needs
Recognises a new product can increase revenue or competitiveness
application_max_2: Links the tablet to the 18,000 existing households or $2.3 million revenue
Links the $6.50 price point or 3-month supply to incremental sales potential

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Fernbrook Cleaning Co may face if it proceeds to the national launch in March.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Developing new products is costly and the outcome is uncertain [k]; Fernbrook has already spent $260,000 and needs a further $150,000 for the trial run, so a failed launch would write off $410,000 [app]; this matters because the loss would reduce retained profit and limit funds available to support the core liquid detergent range [an]. Problem 2: Product weaknesses found in testing may not be fixed in time [k]; 4 of 30 trial households reported that the tablets dissolved too slowly, so a March launch could trigger complaints and returns [app]; this could damage Fernbrook's reputation and reduce sales of its existing detergents as customers lose trust in the brand [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises development costs and uncertainty of success
Recognises that unresolved design flaws cause complaints or returns
application_max_2: Uses the $260,000 spent and $150,000 trial-run cost
Uses the 4 of 30 slow-dissolving trial households
analysis_max_2: Explains impact of failure on retained profit or core range
Explains impact of complaints on brand reputation and existing sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernbrook Cleaning Co should proceed to the national launch in March? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding makes sense because Fernbrook has already invested heavily [k]; it has spent $260,000 and faces a further $150,000, totalling around $410,000 [app]; walking away would waste that investment, whereas a launch into the growing eco refill market could add a profitable new line and strengthen the brand with 18,000 existing households [an]. However, the trial flaw is a serious warning [k]; 4 of 30 households found the tablets dissolved too slowly, and launching in March without reformulation risks disappointing early adopters [app]; poor first impressions could trigger complaints, damage the brand and drag down sales of the $2.3 million core detergent business [an]. Overall, Fernbrook should delay the March launch briefly to fix the dissolution problem and retest rather than abandon the project entirely [eval]; this protects the $410,000 committed while avoiding a damaging failed launch [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands development costs and sunk investment
Understands the risk of launching an unproven product
application_max_2: Uses the $260,000 and $150,000 figures
Uses the 4 of 30 slow-dissolving households or March timing
analysis_max_2: Analyses the upside of launching into the eco refill trend
Analyses the downside of complaints or brand damage to the core range
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options
Considers a middle course such as delaying rather than abandoning

scenario_stem:
Granary & Grain Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has made traditional wheat pasta for 12 years. Last year it launched VerdeProtein, a plant-based protein pasta aimed at gym-goers and vegetarians, after spending $340,000 on two years of development. The company employs 48 staff and VerdeProtein generated just $75,000 in its first 6 months.

VerdeProtein packs contain 28g of protein per 100g, roughly double traditional wheat pasta. VerdeProtein is now stocked in 120 supermarkets, and sales in July reached 5,600 packs at $2.80 each, so the product is in the introduction stage of the product life cycle. Only 22% of shoppers surveyed could identify the brand. The marketing manager controls a $60,000 budget for promotion during the introduction stage.

questions.question_text: Define the 'introduction stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The introduction stage is the first stage of a product's life cycle after launch, when the product is first offered to the market and sales are usually low because awareness is limited and customers have not yet tried it. Promotion and distribution are still being built up and the product often makes losses at this stage. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies it as the launch stage when sales are low
Notes that awareness or distribution is still being built

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sales of VerdeProtein are likely to be low during the introduction stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In the introduction stage the product is new to the market and customer awareness is low [k]; only 22% of shoppers surveyed by Granary & Grain could identify VerdeProtein [app]. Reason 2: Consumers are reluctant to buy an unfamiliar product without proof or promotion [k]; VerdeProtein is stocked in 120 supermarkets and July sales reached just 5,600 packs at $2.80 each, so customer habit and shelf presence are still developing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that awareness is low for a newly launched product
Recognises that customers are reluctant to try unknown products
application_max_2: Uses the 22% brand-awareness figure
Uses the 120 supermarkets or 5,600 July packs figure

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits VerdeProtein could gain from strong promotional support during the introduction stage.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Promotion increases awareness and trial among the target market [k]; allocating part of the $60,000 budget to social media and in-store tasting could lift the 22% recognition figure and persuade gym-goers to try VerdeProtein [app]; wider trial would generate word of mouth and repeat purchases, building early momentum as the product moves towards growth [an]. Benefit 2: Promotion can shift demand and help recover development costs [k]; with July sales of 5,600 packs at $2.80 producing only about $15,680 a month, stronger promotion could close the gap on the $340,000 development spend faster [app]; rising sales also reassure supermarkets to keep stocking the product and avoid delisting [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that promotion builds awareness and trial
Recognises that promotion can lift sales or recover costs
application_max_2: Uses the $60,000 promotional budget or 22% awareness figure
Uses the 5,600 July packs or $2.80 price figure
analysis_max_2: Explains how trial leads to repeat purchase and growth
Explains how rising sales support supermarket listings and faster recovery of costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Granary & Grain Foods Ltd should spend the full $60,000 promoting VerdeProtein during the introduction stage? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Spending now is justified because promotion matters most in the introduction stage [k]; with only 22% of shoppers recognising VerdeProtein and just $75,000 of revenue in 6 months, investment is needed before rivals copy the recipe [app]; allocating the $60,000 across social media and in-store tasting could build awareness and trial, moving VerdeProtein towards growth and protecting the $340,000 spent on development [an]. However, the introduction stage usually brings losses [k]; sales of 5,600 packs in July at $2.80 yield only around $15,680 a month [app], so committing all $60,000 at once could strain cash flow when returns are unproven, and poorly targeted spending aimed at gym-goers may be wasted [an]. Overall, Granary & Grain should spend the $60,000 but in stages, linked to awareness and sales milestones [eval]; this balances the need to build the new brand against financial prudence while the product is unproven [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands promotion is most critical at introduction
Understands introduction-stage losses and cash-flow pressure
application_max_2: Uses the 22% awareness, $75,000 6-month revenue or 5,600 July packs figure
Uses the $60,000 budget or $340,000 development cost figure
analysis_max_2: Analyses how promotion could build awareness and move VerdeProtein towards growth
Analyses the risk of overspending or targeting errors draining cash flow
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options
Considers a staged spending approach linked to milestones

scenario_stem:
Wildroot Brew Co is a private limited company in Country X that launched a fermented kombucha drink 18 months ago. Bottle sales have risen from 30,000 in its first quarter to 190,000 in the latest quarter, and the company employs 26 staff. The product is in the growth stage of the product life cycle. Wildroot's kombucha is brewed from organic tea, raw sugar and live cultures at its plant in Country X.

Wildroot sells through 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per 500ml bottle. Profit last year was $180,000. A rival brand, Zing, plans a similar kombucha launch in 6 months. The owners must decide whether to invest $400,000 of retained profit in extra brewing tanks or hold capacity and raise the price to $3.60.

questions.question_text: Define the 'growth stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The growth stage is the phase in which a product's sales and profits rise rapidly as awareness spreads, the product is accepted by the market and distribution widens. Competitors often enter the market at this stage as the product proves successful. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies rapid growth in sales or profits
Notes rising customer acceptance or widening distribution

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wildroot Brew Co's kombucha sales are rising rapidly in the growth stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In the growth stage early buyers accept the product and word of mouth spreads awareness [k]; bottle sales have risen from 30,000 in Wildroot's first quarter to 190,000 in the latest quarter [app]. Reason 2: Wider distribution makes the product easy to buy [k]; Wildroot is stocked in 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains, so growing numbers of customers can buy a 500ml bottle at $3.20 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises growing acceptance and word-of-mouth awareness
Recognises that wider distribution increases sales
application_max_2: Uses the 30,000 to 190,000 bottle sales rise
Uses the 340 independent health stores, 2 supermarket chains or $3.20 price

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Wildroot Brew Co could gain by investing $400,000 in extra brewing tanks now.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Extra capacity lets the business meet rising demand and avoid lost sales [k]; with quarterly sales up from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles, current tanks are stretched, so extra capacity would let Wildroot fill every order before rival Zing launches in 6 months [app]; this would strengthen supermarket relationships and secure shelf space that might otherwise go to competitors [an]. Benefit 2: Higher volume spreads fixed costs and lifts profit [k]; increasing output to serve the 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per bottle would grow revenue above its current level and raise the $180,000 profit [app]; economies of scale on ingredients and bottling would further reduce unit costs and improve margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that capacity expansion meets rising demand
Recognises that higher volume can reduce unit costs or raise profit
application_max_2: Uses the 30,000 to 190,000 quarterly sales rise or Zing's 6-month launch
Uses the 340 independent health stores, 2 supermarket chains, $3.20 price or $180,000 profit
analysis_max_2: Explains link between capacity and supermarket relationships or shelf space
Explains how rising output or scale improves sales and margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Wildroot Brew Co should invest $400,000 of retained profit in extra brewing tanks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing is attractive because the growth stage is the moment to capture market share [k]; sales have risen from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles per quarter and distribution spans 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains [app]; added capacity would let Wildroot supply demand fully, lock in volume and defend supermarket shelf space before Zing launches in 6 months, building on the $180,000 profit already achieved [an]. However, the investment carries real risk [k]; the $400,000 would come from retained profit, and if Zing wins share or consumer tastes change, Wildroot could be left with excess capacity and lower cash reserves [app]; raising the price to $3.60 to protect margins might slow the sales momentum that makes expansion worthwhile [an]. Overall, Wildroot should invest the $400,000 now [eval]; the sixfold sales rise and the imminent rival launch make speed more valuable than preserving cash, and failing to expand risks permanently losing supermarket shelf space [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands the competitive logic of investing at the growth stage
Understands the risk of tying up retained profit in capacity
application_max_2: Uses the 30,000 to 190,000 sales rise, 340 stores or 2 supermarket chains
Uses the $400,000 investment, Zing's 6-month launch or the $3.60 price rise option
analysis_max_2: Analyses how capacity supports demand and market-share defence
Analyses the risk of excess capacity or price rises slowing momentum
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options
Considers timing relative to Zing's entry or the price-rise alternative

scenario_stem:
Amberfields Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that produces QuickQuick instant noodle pots. The brand is 14 years old and sales have been flat at around 900,000 pots a year for 3 years, placing the market at maturity. The company employs 72 staff and QuickQuick generated $2.7 million revenue last year, sold as 112,500 cases of 8 pots at $24 per case.

Amberfields holds a 16% share of the instant noodle market, down from 21% four years ago, as two rivals undercut its price by $0.10 per pot. The marketing manager must recommend an extension strategy, a new spicy variant and festival multipack, or a permanent wholesale price cut to match rivals. The board has $150,000 available.

questions.question_text: Define the 'maturity stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The maturity stage is the phase in which sales growth slows and levels off as the market becomes saturated with the product and competition intensifies. Sales remain high but plateau, and businesses typically focus on defending market share and extending the product's profitable life. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies sales growth slowing or levelling off
Notes high but flat sales amid heavy competition

questions.question_text: Explain two features of the maturity stage of the product life cycle shown by QuickQuick.
questions.model_answer: Feature 1: Sales are high but flat, with little growth [k]; QuickQuick sales have been flat at around 900,000 pots a year for 3 years [app]. Feature 2: Competition is intense and prices come under pressure [k]; two rivals undercut QuickQuick by $0.10 per pot and its share has slipped from 21% to 16% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises plateauing or flat sales at maturity
Recognises intensified competition and price pressure
application_max_2: Uses the flat 900,000 pots a year figure
Uses the $0.10 undercut or 21% to 16% share slide

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of an extension strategy for QuickQuick instant noodle pots.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: An extension strategy prolongs the product life cycle and defends revenue [k]; a new spicy variant and festival multipack could reverse the share slide from 21% to 16% without resorting to a permanent $0.10 price cut, keeping QuickQuick relevant as tastes change [app]; maintaining sales of around 900,000 pots a year would protect $2.7 million of revenue and the jobs of 72 staff [an]. Benefit 2: It creates fresh promotional opportunities at relatively low cost [k]; with the board's $150,000 available, new variants can be advertised and displayed in store to win back lapsed buyers [app]; renewed attention can lift repeat purchase rates and slow the drift towards saturation [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that extension strategies prolong the life cycle or defend share
Recognises extension strategies create promotional freshness
application_max_2: Uses the 21% to 16% share slide, 900,000 pots or $2.7 million revenue
Uses the $150,000 board budget or the spicy variant and festival multipack
analysis_max_2: Explains how variants protect revenue and jobs or slow decline
Explains how promotion refreshes the brand and drives repeat purchase

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfields Foods Ltd should use an extension strategy rather than cut its wholesale price permanently? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An extension strategy is the stronger option [k]; a new spicy variant and festival multipack would refresh the brand and appeal to the 900,000 pots a year that QuickQuick still sells, rebuilding the share that slipped from 21% to 16% without eroding margins across the whole range [app]; focused promotion using the $150,000 budget protects the $2.7 million revenue and avoids a $0.10 cut lowering profit on every case sold [an]. However, a price cut responds to rivals immediately [k]; matching the $0.10 undercut would win back price-sensitive buyers who switched and could restore volume quickly, an outcome the $150,000 extension plan cannot guarantee [app]; deep cuts, though, risk a price war and signal that QuickQuick is a cheap brand, weakening its position further [an]. Overall, Amberfields should choose the extension strategy over a permanent price cut [eval]; it protects profit per pot and rebuilds brand appeal, whereas a permanent cut sacrifices long-term profitability for only temporary volume [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands extension strategies refresh the product or defend share
Understands price cuts respond to rivals but erode margins
application_max_2: Uses the 21% to 16% share slide, 900,000 pots or $2.7 million revenue
Uses the $150,000 budget, $0.10 undercut or spicy variant and festival multipack
analysis_max_2: Analyses how variants and promotion rebuild share without cutting margin
Analyses how permanent price cuts affect profit or invite a price war
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options
Considers short-term volume recovery against long-term margin damage

scenario_stem:
Cascade Beverages is a private limited company in Country X that bottles Cascade Cola, launched 19 years ago. The market is now saturated: sales peaked at 18 million bottles in 2021 and last year reached 12.5 million bottles at $1.50 each, a fall of over 30%. The company employs 88 staff.

The marketing director proposes an extension strategy built on redesign: Cascade Zero, a sugar-free cola in new recyclable bottles, at a development and promotion cost of $380,000. The alternative is launching two new flavours in the existing packaging at $180,000. Cascade Zero would add an estimated $0.35 of extra cost per bottle, and the board must choose between the two options. Cascade plans to keep production at its existing Country X bottling plant whichever option it selects.

questions.question_text: Define the 'saturation stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The saturation stage is the point at which the market is full of the product and virtually everyone who wants one already has it, so sales peak and then begin to fall. Further growth can only come from extension strategies or from reaching new customer segments. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the market as full of the product
Notes sales peaked and began to fall

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Cascade Beverages wants to use an extension strategy at this stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The market is saturated, so organic growth has stalled [k]; sales peaked at 18 million bottles in 2021 and have fallen to 12.5 million last year, a drop of over 30% [app]. Reason 2: Extension strategies refresh the product and attract new buyers [k]; a sugar-free variant in new recyclable bottles could appeal to health-conscious customers, while new flavours could target different tastes [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises that saturated markets stall organic growth
Recognises that extension strategies refresh products and attract buyers
application_max_2: Uses the 18 million peak versus 12.5 million bottles or over 30% fall
Uses the sugar-free Cascade Zero or recyclable bottles proposal

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Cascade Beverages could face with the proposed extension strategies.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Extension strategies require heavy investment with no guaranteed payoff [k]; Cascade Zero would cost $380,000 against $180,000 for the two new flavours, and the extra $0.35 per bottle would raise unit costs [app]; if the sugar-free cola fails to win share, the larger spend would intensify losses in a market already down over 30% [an]. Problem 2: New flavours can fail if they miss customer tastes [k]; the existing-packaging option at $180,000 offers little shelf differentiation in a crowded cola market, so trial may be slow [app]; weak adoption would leave Cascade with disappointing sales and less money for future launches [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises heavy investment and uncertain payoff
Recognises new variants may miss customer tastes
application_max_2: Uses the $380,000 Cascade Zero cost or $0.35 extra per bottle
Uses the $180,000 two-flavour alternative
analysis_max_2: Explains consequence of failure in a falling market on losses or viability
Explains how slow trial undermines extension success or future launches

questions.question_text: Do you think Cascade Beverages should launch Cascade Zero in redesigned recyclable bottles rather than two new flavours? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cascade Zero is the stronger choice [k]; a sugar-free cola in redesigned recyclable bottles targets two powerful trends, health and sustainability, and would stand out on shelves in a saturated market where sales have fallen over 30% to 12.5 million bottles a year [app]; a visible, differentiated relaunch could rebuild the brand, attract new buyers and restart growth, justifying the $380,000 investment despite the extra $0.35 per bottle [an]. However, the two new flavours cost only $180,000 [k]; launching them in existing packaging keeps costs low and spreads risk across two products, which is safer if health trends shift again or Cascade Zero underperforms [app]; a failed relaunch would leave the board having spent more than double for no gain [an]. Overall, Cascade should back Cascade Zero [eval]; the differentiation and brand revival it offers outweigh the higher cost, provided the board sets clear sales targets and reviews performance after 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands how redesigned differentiated extensions rebuild brands
Understands the cost and risk trade-offs between options
application_max_2: Uses the over 30% fall to 12.5 million bottles or $380,000 Cascade Zero cost
Uses the $180,000 two-flavour alternative or $0.35 extra cost
analysis_max_2: Analyses how differentiation and trends could restart growth
Analyses the risk of overspending or underperformance on relaunch
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options
Considers monitoring and review as a condition of the decision

scenario_stem:
Bridgewater Office Machines Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has manufactured office fax machines for 16 years, employing 30 staff. Unit sales peaked at 14,000 machines in 2019 and fell to 3,600 last year as businesses switched to email and scanning. Revenue fell from $1.4 million to $380,000 over the same period.

The machines are now in the decline stage of the product life cycle, and Bridgewater holds $140,000 of unsold stock. The managing director proposes an extension strategy, a Wi-Fi internet fax model costing $220,000 to develop, or stopping fax production and converting the workshop to servicing machines and selling scanners, which would affect 18 production workers. Bridgewater wrote down $60,000 of unsold stock last year alone.

questions.question_text: Define the 'decline stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The decline stage is the final phase of the product life cycle in which sales and profits fall steadily as the product becomes obsolete or is replaced by newer alternatives or changing customer tastes. Businesses may withdraw, extend or replace the product. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies sales and profits falling in this phase
Notes the product becomes obsolete or is replaced by alternatives

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why fax machine sales have fallen into the decline stage for Bridgewater Office Machines.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Technological change has made the product obsolete [k]; businesses have switched to email and document scanning, so Bridgewater's sales fell from a peak of 14,000 machines in 2019 to just 3,600 last year [app]. Reason 2: Customers are leaving the category altogether [k]; revenue dropped from $1.4 million to $380,000 over the same period, leaving Bridgewater with $140,000 of unsold stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises technological obsolescence as a cause of decline
Recognises that falling demand reduces revenue and leaves unsold stock
application_max_2: Uses the 14,000 to 3,600 machines sales fall
Uses the $1.4 million to $380,000 revenue fall or $140,000 stock figure

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Bridgewater Office Machines would face if it developed the Wi-Fi internet fax model.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Development is expensive and returns are uncertain [k]; the Wi-Fi fax model would cost $220,000 at a time when revenue has fallen to $380,000 and $140,000 of stock is unsold [app]; if the new model fails, Bridgewater would be left with even deeper losses and no rescue for the core fax business [an]. Problem 2: The fax segment itself is shrinking [k]; even a Wi-Fi fax targets a category collapsing from 14,000 to 3,600 units a year, so it may only cannibalise existing orders rather than win new customers [app]; spending $220,000 to prolong a dying product could delay the necessary shift into servicing and scanners [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises development cost and uncertain return
Recognises shrinking markets limit extension potential
application_max_2: Uses the $220,000 development cost or $380,000 revenue figure
Uses the 14,000 to 3,600 units fall or $140,000 unsold stock
analysis_max_2: Explains consequence of failure on losses or viability
Explains cannibalisation risk and delayed strategic shift

questions.question_text: Do you think Bridgewater Office Machines should develop the Wi-Fi internet fax model? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Developing the Wi-Fi fax has some merit [k]; it would extend the life of an established product and appeal to the shrinking base of offices that still require fax confirmation, differentiating Bridgewater from pure hardware rivals [app]; at $220,000 the spend is significant but not ruinous against $380,000 of revenue, and success would clear some of the $140,000 stock backlog while protecting the 18 production workers [an]. However, the decline stage indicates demand will not recover [k]; sales collapsed from 14,000 to 3,600 units and revenue from $1.4 million to $380,000, so more investment in fax may only delay the inevitable [app]; converting the workshop to servicing and scanners addresses a stable, growing need and would secure the 30 staff more sustainably [an]. Overall, Bridgewater should stop fax production and convert rather than develop the Wi-Fi model [eval]; the collapse in demand shows extension is unlikely to succeed, and conversion repositions the business around what customers now buy [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Understands the rationale and limits of extension strategies
Understands the logic of withdrawing from declining products
application_max_2: Uses the 14,000 to 3,600 units or $1.4 million to $380,000 revenue collapse
Uses the $220,000 Wi-Fi cost, $140,000 stock or 18 production workers
analysis_max_2: Analyses what the extension would achieve and for whom
Analyses why demand collapse makes withdrawal the stronger option
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options

scenario_stem:
Hearthfield Botanics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that sells Nettle & Sage herbal shampoo bars. The brand launched 8 years ago and sales reached 600,000 bars a year at $8.50, but have plateaued for 2 years. The company employs 44 staff and repeat purchases have slipped from 38% to 29% of customers over 12 months.

The marketing manager is weighing an extension strategy. Option one refreshes the domestic range: 3 new scents and a 50g travel-size bar at $4.00, costing a combined $150,000. Option two exports Nettle & Sage to Country Z with licensing and promotion costing $150,000. Local rival Brightmane has just launched a new scent range with heavy television and social media advertising. The manager must present a final recommendation to the board within 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define an 'extension strategy'.
questions.model_answer: An extension strategy is a marketing action used to prolong the maturity or saturation stage of the product life cycle, such as changing the product, its packaging, promotion, price or market, so that sales decline more slowly or rise again instead of entering decline. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies it as prolonging the product life cycle
Gives an example such as new variants, packaging, promotion or new markets

questions.question_text: Explain two extension strategies Hearthfield Botanics could use for Nettle & Sage shampoo bars.
questions.model_answer: Strategy 1: Product variation refreshes the range and attracts new buyers [k]; adding 3 new scents and a 50g travel-size bar at $4.00 could tempt lapsed customers and reverse the slip in repeat purchases from 38% to 29% [app]. Strategy 2: Entering a new geographical market extends the life cycle [k]; exporting Nettle & Sage to Country Z, costed at $150,000 for licensing and promotion, would expose the bars to customers who have never encountered them [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises product variation as an extension strategy
Recognises entering new markets as an extension strategy
application_max_2: Uses the 3 new scents, 50g travel-size bar or $4.00 price details
Uses the Country Z export option or the 38% to 29% repeat-purchase slip

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of an extension strategy for Hearthfield Botanics.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: An extension strategy protects revenue without abandoning the brand [k]; with sales flat at 600,000 bars a year at $8.50, either option could restart growth instead of accepting decline [app]; this secures cash flow and the jobs of 44 staff while Hearthfield develops its next product [an]. Benefit 2: Extension strategies are often cheaper than launching an entirely new product [k]; the domestic refresh costs a combined $150,000 and builds on a proven formula, distribution and quality [app]; re-engaging existing loyal buyers, who drove repeat purchases of 38% before slipping to 29%, is more efficient than winning brand-new customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises extension protects revenue or prolongs the life cycle
Recognises extension is cheaper than a new product launch
application_max_2: Uses the flat 600,000 bars at $8.50 or 44 staff details
Uses the $150,000 domestic refresh cost or the 38% to 29% repeat slip
analysis_max_2: Explains how restart of growth secures cash flow or jobs
Explains efficiency of re-engaging existing loyal buyers

questions.question_text: Do you think Hearthfield Botanics should prioritise exporting to Country Z rather than refreshing the domestic range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting is ambitious but uncertain [k]; Country Z would give Nettle & Sage entirely new customers instead of conceding the domestic market to Brightmane's heavy advertising, and long-run growth could outstrip a domestic refresh [app]; however, entry requires licensing, promotion and compliance costing $150,000 with no guarantee of distribution, and overseas failures can absorb cash faster than home [an]. By contrast, refreshing the domestic range, 3 new scents plus a 50g travel-size at $4.00, costs the same $150,000 but acts on known data [k]; repeat purchases have already slipped from 38% to 29%, so new scents and a cheaper entry-size could reactivate existing buyers of the 600,000 bars sold each year [app]; it also directly answers Brightmane's launch rather than abandoning domestic shelf space [an]. Overall, Hearthfield should refresh the domestic range first [eval]; the equal cost is outweighed by lower risk and quicker returns, and exporting can follow once domestic momentum recovers [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ambercup Coffee Co is a private limited company in Country X that roasts bagged ground coffee, with revenue of $1.6 million last year and 28 employees. Demand for ready-to-drink cold brew is growing by 24% a year. Ambercup estimates $280,000 to develop its own cold brew can range, including $90,000 for canning-line trials and $70,000 for market testing. The cans would be 250ml aluminium, sold through convenience stores, supermarkets and gyms.

If successful, the cold brew range could add $520,000 of revenue in its first year. However, 3 of the last 8 new drink launches in Country X failed within 18 months. Ambercup would also need $150,000 for a national promotional launch, and the owners must decide whether to develop the cold brew range.

questions.question_text: Define 'research and development'.
questions.model_answer: Research and development is the systematic process of investigating customer needs and technologies and applying findings to create new products, improve existing ones and design effective production methods before commercial launch. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies it as systematic investigation of needs or technologies
Notes it is used to create or improve products before launch

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Ambercup Coffee Co of developing the cold brew range.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A growing new product diversifies revenue and reduces reliance on one range [k]; with cold brew demand growing by 24% a year, Ambercup could tap a new segment and add an estimated $520,000 of first-year revenue [app]. Benefit 2: A successful launch can strengthen the brand and competitive position [k]; adding cold brew to Ambercup's bagged coffee range, which generated $1.6 million last year, would create a one-stop choice for existing wholesale customers and raise average order value [app].

Uses the $1.6 million bagged coffee revenue or roasting context

questions.question_text: Explain two costs Ambercup Coffee Co would incur by developing the cold brew range.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Development and testing costs are substantial before any sale is made [k]; Ambercup must commit $280,000, including $90,000 for canning-line trials and $70,000 for market testing, about 17.5% of its $1.6 million revenue [app]; if the launch fails, this money is unrecoverable [an]. Cost 2: Promotion and launch costs add further financial strain [k]; a national promotional launch would need another $150,000, taking total exposure to around $430,000 [app]; combined with 3 of the last 8 launches failing within 18 months, the risk of cash-flow pressure and wasted spend is significant [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ambercup Coffee Co should develop the cold brew range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Developing cold brew is attractive [k]; demand is growing by 24% a year and first-year revenue could reach $520,000, revitalising a bagged coffee business with $1.6 million of revenue and attracting younger buyers [app]; the total commitment of about $430,000 could be recovered within a year if sales materialise, and early entry would beat rivals to shelf space [an]. However, the risks are real [k]; with 3 of the last 8 new drink launches failing within 18 months, Ambercup could lose the $280,000 development spend plus the $150,000 launch budget, squeezing profit and the existing roasting operation [app]; if shoppers favour conventional iced coffee or bigger brands copy the idea, sales could fall far short of $520,000 [an]. Overall, Ambercup should proceed, but only after the market testing phase proves customer demand [eval]; a stage-gate decision after the $70,000 tests means money is committed only when viable, balancing a growing market against the known high failure rate [eval].

scenario_stem:
Emberglow Candle Co is a private limited company in Country X making scented candles for 6 years. For the first 4 years it sold own-brand candles in gift shops at $14, with modest sales. Last year it relaunched as the premium brand Maison Ember, with luxury packaging and a stronger fragrance story, selling 180,000 candles at $22 each and lifting revenue to $3.96 million. The relaunch involved rebuilding the name, scent profiles and artwork over 6 months with a packaging design agency.

Repeat purchases rose from 19% to 34% after the relaunch, and the company employs 39 staff. Rival Lumen Homeware sells similar candles at $12. Moving Maison Ember into supermarkets at a lower $9 price would double volume but may damage the premium brand image Emberglow has built.

questions.question_text: Define 'brand image'.
questions.model_answer: Brand image is the set of beliefs, perceptions and feelings consumers hold about a particular brand, formed by its name, logo, packaging, advertising, quality and customer experiences. It shapes whether buyers notice, trust and choose that brand over competitors. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies brand image as consumer perception or beliefs about a brand
Notes it is shaped by name, packaging, advertising, quality or experience

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a strong brand image can help Emberglow Candle Co.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: A strong brand image increases loyalty and repeat purchases [k]; after the Maison Ember relaunch, repeat purchases rose from 19% to 34%, showing customers formed a favourable premium perception [app]. Way 2: It allows the business to charge a higher price [k]; Maison Ember sells 180,000 candles at $22 each against a rival at $12, lifting revenue to $3.96 million [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises strong brand image increases loyalty or repeat purchase
Recognises strong brand image supports premium pricing
application_max_2: Uses the 19% to 34% repeat-purchase rise
Uses the $22 price, $12 rival price, 180,000 candles or $3.96 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems that might result from moving Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A much lower price erodes premium positioning [k]; selling Maison Ember at $9 instead of the $22 gift-shop price signals a mass-market product and clashes with the luxury packaging and fragrance story behind the relaunch [app]; supermarket bargain displays could make loyal gift-shop buyers question the value of what they paid [an]. Problem 2: Supermarket channels cut profit per candle [k]; moving to volume at $9 doubles volume but takes far less margin per unit than $22, squeezing profitability unless costs fall sharply [app]; the $3.96 million revenue stream could shift from high-margin gift shops to high-volume, low-margin sales, so total profit may fall even if revenue doubles [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises low prices erode premium positioning or perceived exclusivity
Recognises supermarket margins or volume-margin trade-offs

Uses the $3.96 million revenue or doubled-volume framing

Explains how margin shift can reduce total profit despite higher volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Emberglow Candle Co should move Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Supermarket distribution is tempting [k]; at $9 Maison Ember would undercut rival Lumen Homeware at $12 and roughly double volume, lifting revenue well beyond the current $3.96 million and placing the brand in front of far more shoppers [app]; for a young brand, supermarket shelf space would raise awareness and introduce Maison Ember to a wider demographic [an]. However, it risks the premium image [k]; discounting to $9 erodes the exclusivity created by luxury packaging and the fragrance story that justified $22 gift-shop pricing and drove repeat purchases from 19% to 34% [app]; cannibalising gift-shop sales at less than half the margin could reduce total profit despite higher volume, and recovering premium positioning later is very difficult [an]. Overall, Emberglow should not move Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9 [eval]; the brand's value rests on premium scarcity and perception, so a separate value line, not the Maison Ember range itself, would be the safer route if supermarket entry is ever pursued [eval].

scenario_stem:
Sunhaven Vitamins Ltd is a private limited company in Country X selling children's multivitamin gummies. It sells 900,000 bottles a year at $11.50, generating $10.35 million in revenue, with 26 employees. Pharmacies are the main seller, and each bottle contains 60 gummies, roughly a two-month supply for a child aged 4 to 10. Complaints show 3,800 opened bottles were found by children despite child-resistant caps, including one near-miss incident.

Sunhaven plans a redesigned pack: a resealable child-safe pouch with bold dosing information and bright fruit graphics, costing $110,000 plus $0.22 more per unit. Retooling for the changeover would cost $75,000. Parents in trials rated the new pack 4.6 out of 5, and pharmacy sales could rise by an estimated 12%.

questions.question_text: Define 'packaging'.
questions.model_answer: Packaging is the materials and design used to contain, wrap, protect and present a product for sale. It serves functional purposes such as protection and safety and marketing purposes such as attracting attention, providing information and reinforcing brand identity. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies packaging as materials or design used to contain or protect the product
Notes functional or marketing roles such as safety, information or branding

questions.question_text: Explain two roles of packaging for Sunhaven's children's multivitamin gummies.
questions.model_answer: Role 1: Packaging protects the product and keeps children safe [k]; the redesigned resealable child-safe pouch directly addresses the 3,800 opened-bottle complaints and the near-miss incident, reducing the chance of harm [app]. Role 2: Packaging communicates information and promotes the product [k]; bold dosing information shows parents the correct dose clearly, while bright fruit graphics make the product appealing, with trial parents rating the pack 4.6 out of 5 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises protection or safety as a packaging role
Recognises information or promotion as a packaging role
application_max_2: Uses the 3,800 opened-bottle complaints or near-miss incident
Uses the bold dosing information, bright fruit graphics or 4.6 out of 5 rating

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Sunhaven Vitamins would gain from the packaging redesign.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Improved safety can cut complaints and liability [k]; a resealable child-safe pouch would directly address the 3,800 opened-bottle incidents, protecting children and reducing the risk of expensive claims or product recalls [app]; this safeguards the brand's reputation with parents, the key buyers in pharmacy purchases [an]. Benefit 2: The redesign can lift sales and profit [k]; trials scored the new pack 4.6 out of 5 and pharmacy sales could rise by an estimated 12% on $10.35 million of revenue [app]; clearer dosing and stronger shelf stand-out use packaging as promotion, encouraging repeat purchase and cushioning the $0.22 extra unit cost [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recognises improved safety reduces complaints or liability
Recognises redesign can lift sales or repeat purchase
application_max_2: Uses the 3,800 opened-bottle incidents or child-safe pouch
Uses the 4.6 out of 5 rating, 12% estimated pharmacy sales rise or $10.35 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Explains how safety protects reputation and parental trust
Explains how packaging promotion supports repeat purchase or absorbs unit cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunhaven Vitamins should go ahead with the packaging redesign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The redesign is justified [k]; child safety is non-negotiable, and the current child-resistant caps have failed, with 3,800 opened bottles found by children and one near-miss, so a resealable child-safe pouch directly fixes a real risk [app]; together with bold dosing information, bright fruit graphics and a 4.6 out of 5 parent rating, the change would build trust and could lift pharmacy sales by an estimated 12% on $10.35 million of revenue [an]. However, the costs are significant [k]; the $110,000 development spend plus $75,000 retooling and $0.22 more per unit will squeeze margins on 900,000 bottles a year, roughly $198,000 of extra annual unit cost before any sales increase [app]; if the projected 12% uplift does not appear, the investment will not pay back quickly [an]. Overall, Sunhaven should proceed with the redesign [eval]; the safety imperative and strong trial feedback outweigh the $0.22 cost increase, and for a children's health product reputational damage is far costlier than the redesign [eval].

Understands the cost implications of a redesign
